opus-5.5.text:
I think generality here has a few layers.

The first is in the tools themselves. Once a model can use a search engine, a code interpreter, a browser, or a file system, its action space expands enormously. Many tasks that looked very different, like writing a research report, debugging a codebase, or analyzing data, turn out to share the same underlying pattern: you observe the environment, decide what to do next, take an action, get feedback, and adjust. So the generality isn't that we hand-design a solution for each task. It's that a single loop of reasoning and acting can cover a huge range of tasks.

The second layer, which I think matters more, is the "multiple turns" part. Single-step question answering mostly tests what the model already knows. Multi-turn tool use tests whether the model can keep a long-horizon goal in mind and recover when something goes wrong. Real tasks are almost never solved in one shot. You search, the result is not quite right, you refine the query, you discover the problem was framed wrongly, and you go back. The ability to keep pushing over tens or even hundreds of steps without drifting is a very general capability. It transfers across domains in a way that narrow skills don't.

The third layer concerns how we train it. If you only do imitation, the model learns to copy trajectories and breaks as soon as the environment differs a bit. But if you train end to end with reinforcement learning in real environments, rewarding the outcome rather than prescribing every step, the model learns more fundamental things: when to gather more information, when to verify, when to change strategy. Those behaviors generalize. In a sense, the agent learns how to learn inside the task, and that's where I think the real generality comes from.

So my view is that agentic capability isn't a separate application layered on top of the model. It's a natural extension of intelligence itself. Intelligence was never just about answering in one step. It's about achieving goals in a complex environment over time, and multi-turn tool use is the most direct way to put that into practice.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the way to understand it is that an agent using tools over many turns is really just a model interacting with a much richer environment than a single prompt. Once you give a model the ability to call tools, observe the result, and decide what to do next, the task is no longer "produce one answer." The task becomes "produce a trajectory," and the same underlying capability has to cover search, code execution, reading files, operating a browser, and so on. That is where generality comes from. The model is not learning a specific workflow. It is learning a general policy for how to act when the environment talks back.

What makes this different from earlier notions of generality is that the feedback loop is inside the task. In a single-turn setting, the model's mistakes are invisible to it. In a multi-turn tool setting, a wrong assumption shows up immediately as an error message, an empty search result, a failed test. So the model has to learn to update its beliefs, to recover, to re-plan. That skill transfers across domains much more than any particular tool does. If a model can genuinely do error recovery in a coding environment, a lot of that carries over to research or to operating software, because the structure of the problem is the same: act, observe, correct.

The other point I would make is that generality here is largely a property of the training distribution, not just the architecture. If you train on a narrow set of tools and tasks, you get an agent that looks capable on benchmarks but breaks when the environment changes slightly. If you train across many environments with diverse tools, long horizons, and real consequences for actions, the model starts learning the abstract thing, which is something like "how to accomplish goals under uncertainty with partial information." That is closer to what we actually mean by intelligence.

So I would summarize it like this. Tools are the interface, multi-turn is the structure, and generality is the ability to reuse a single policy across very different interfaces and structures. The hard part is not giving the model tools. The hard part is making sure what it learns from one environment is the general lesson rather than the specific one.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is whether the agent can handle new tasks with the same underlying capabilities, rather than whether it has access to a lot of tools. You could connect a model to a hundred tools, but if every workflow has to be specified in advance, its generality is still limited.

With multiple turns, the model has to close a loop: decide what to do, use a tool, interpret the result, and then decide what to do next. The result may contradict its original assumption. A tool may fail. Or it may discover that it needs more information. So the important capability is adapting its actions while maintaining the overall objective.

That’s why I would look at unfamiliar tasks and unfamiliar combinations of tools. Can the agent work out a useful approach without someone writing the procedure for it? Can it recover from mistakes? And can it recognize when it has actually finished? To me, that is a more meaningful measure of generality than succeeding on a fixed sequence of tool calls.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is whether the agent can keep making progress when the task takes many steps and the next step depends on what it observes. Using a tool once is relatively straightforward. Over multiple turns, the model needs to decide which tool to use, interpret the result, update its understanding, and sometimes recognize that its previous approach was wrong.

So generality is more than the number of tools it can call. It’s whether the same underlying capability transfers across different tools and unfamiliar tasks. If you change the environment or give it a tool it hasn’t seen before, can it understand the interface and use feedback to accomplish the goal?

There’s also a reliability issue. Small mistakes can accumulate over a long sequence of actions. A general agent needs to maintain the goal, track what has actually been established, and recover from errors. I would look at those abilities together, rather than treating successful tool calls as sufficient evidence of generality.
